title: Product Photography at Home: White Background and Lighting — cv.cm
description: DIY product photography: a white sweep or light tent, window or two-light setup, tripod, f/8 to f/11, focus stacking, consistent angles and marketplace-ready photos.
h1: How do you take product photos at home with a white background?
answer: Tape a sheet of white paper from a wall down onto a table to make a curved sweep, set the product on it beside a large window or under two daylight lamps, and put a white card opposite the light. Use a tripod, f/8 to f/11, ISO 100 and a 2 second timer, and brighten the exposure until the background is white but the product keeps detail.

sections.h: What a good product photo needs
body: Shoppers cannot touch the product, so the photo has to answer their questions: what it looks like, what color it really is, how big it is, and what the details feel like. That means three technical goals.

ul: Sharp from front to back, so every edge and label is readable.
Accurate color, so returns do not happen because the item looked different.
A clean, consistent background, so the product is the only thing to look at and a whole catalog looks like a set.

body: None of this needs an expensive studio. A table near a window, white paper, a piece of white card and a tripod are enough for most small and medium products.

body: The curve matters: a smooth bend between floor and wall removes the horizon line behind the product, so the background looks endless. Keep the product 50 cm or more in front of the back wall if you can. The farther it is from the background, the easier it is to light them separately and the softer any shadow on the wall becomes.
White paper only looks white when it gets enough light. With too little light it records as grey, which is the most common problem in home product photos.

sections.h: Light it: window, or two lamps
body: Window light setup. Put the table beside a large window with no direct sun. Light from the side shows the shape of the product. Place a white card or foam board on the opposite side, close to the product, to lighten the shadow side. If the window has direct sun, cover it with a thin white curtain. Turn off ceiling lights so their warm color does not mix with daylight. Shoot at a similar time each day, because window light changes color and strength over the day.
Two-light setup. Use two identical continuous LED panels or flashes so they have the same color.

ol: Key light: at about 45 degrees to one side and slightly above the product, through a diffuser or softbox.
Fill: a white card on the other side, or a second light at lower power, to lighten shadows.
Background: for a pure white background, aim one light at the back wall only, not at the product. The background should be about 1 to 1.5 stops brighter than the front of the product.
Set the exposure for the product first, then raise the background light until the background turns white in the photo but the product edges do not glow.

body: Choose lamps with a daylight color around 5,000 to 5,600 K and a high color rendering index (CRI of 95 or higher if you can), so colors are accurate. Avoid ordinary household bulbs, which are warmer and often uneven in color.

Shiny products such as glass, metal and glossy packaging reflect everything around them. A light tent surrounds them with white, which gives clean reflections. Black cards placed just outside the frame add dark edges that show the outline of clear glass.

body: Stopping down beyond about f/16 makes the whole image slightly softer because of diffraction, so for very small products use focus stacking instead of a tiny aperture.

Check the histogram: the background should touch the right edge, and the product's own graph should end before it. If the camera or phone has a highlight warning (blinking areas), the background may blink, but the product must not.

When you photograph a ring, a watch or a cosmetic bottle from close up, even f/11 may not keep the front and back sharp. Focus stacking solves this: take several photos with the focus moved a little each time, then let software combine the sharp parts.

ol: Put the camera on a tripod and set manual exposure so every frame is identical.
Use f/5.6 to f/11, which camera makers recommend for focus bracketing; it balances depth per frame and sharpness.
Focus on the nearest point of the product and take a frame.
Move the focus slightly farther and take the next frame. Repeat until the farthest point is sharp. Small products often need 5 to 15 frames.
Combine the frames in stacking or editing software. Many recent cameras have a focus bracketing function that moves focus automatically, and some can merge the frames in camera.

body: Nothing may move during the sequence, including the product, the lights and the table. On a phone, true focus stacking needs a special app; for most products, stepping back slightly and cropping gives enough depth instead.

Shoppers compare items side by side, so every product in a store should use the same angles, lens, distance and light. Mark the camera and product positions on the table with tape, and write down the settings.

body: Marketplaces usually have rules for the main image: often a pure white or plain background, the product filling most of the frame, no added text, logos or watermarks, and only the item that is for sale. Size and format rules differ between marketplaces and change over time, so check the current seller guidelines of each platform before a big shoot.

sections.h: Editing, background removal and common mistakes
body: Edit one photo, then apply the same changes to the rest of the set so color and brightness match. Remove dust and scratches; customers notice them in close-ups. Do not change the product's real color or shape.

If the background is not quite white, or you shot on a table at home, you can cut the product out. cv.cm's background remover makes a transparent PNG in the browser, which you can place on pure white or any color. Then use the resize tool to make the size and file weight the platform asks for.

faq.q: Why is my white background grey in product photos?
faq.a: The background did not get enough light, and the camera tried to make the bright scene average grey. Add light to the background or increase exposure by about +1 EV until the background is white while the product still has detail.

faq.q: What aperture is best for product photography?
faq.a: Start at f/8 to f/11 on a camera so the whole product is sharp. Do not go much beyond f/16, which softens detail. For tiny products, use focus stacking.

faq.q: Can I take product photos with my phone?
faq.a: Yes. Use a tripod or clamp, window light or two daylight lamps, the 2x lens, a timer, and lock focus and exposure on the product. Avoid portrait mode for main images, because its blur can cut into product edges.

faq.q: Do I need a lightbox for product photography?
faq.a: Not for most products. A paper sweep by a window with a white card for fill works well. A light tent helps most with small and shiny items such as jewelry and cosmetics, and you can make one from a cardboard box and baking paper.

faq.q: How do I keep product photos consistent?
faq.a: Mark the positions of the camera, lights and product with tape, use manual exposure and custom white balance, keep the same lens and distance, and shoot each batch in one session.
